text: Attributed by the US, UK and South Korean governments to North Korea's Reconnaissance General Bureau, Andariel is described in a July 2024 joint advisory as stealing defense, aerospace and nuclear secrets and funding that work with ransomware against US healthcare. MITRE ATT&CK describes it as a sub-set of Lazarus Group; the advisory does not use that term.

APT-C-60 is the name JPCERT/CC uses for a threat group it says likely carried out spear-phishing attacks on organizations in Japan from August 2024, using fake job-applicant emails and a backdoor called SpyGlace. No government or MITRE source opened for this page says who is behind it.

Attributed by MITRE ATT&CK to PLA Unit 61398 in China, APT1 is the subject of a US indictment of 19 May 2014 charging five Unit 61398 officers with hacking six US organizations. The Department of Justice alleges the aim was commercial gain for China's state-owned firms.

APT18 (MITRE G0026) is described by MITRE ATT&CK as a threat group active since at least 2009, with targets in technology, manufacturing, government and medical sectors. A US health sector briefing (HHS HC3, 2020) lists suspected attribution to China; no advisory, indictment or named sponsor was found.

MITRE ATT&CK describes APT19 (also Codoso) as a Chinese-based group that has targeted defense, finance, legal and other industries, with activity reported in 2014 and 2017. Only MITRE ATT&CK documents this group, no government advisory names it, and MITRE says it is unclear whether APT19 and Deep Panda are the same group.

Attributed by MITRE ATT&CK and by the US Department of Justice (5 March 2025) to a Chinese group, also called Threat Group-3390 and Emissary Panda, that targets governments and companies. The Justice Department charged two men it calls APT27 actors, alleging profit-driven hacking from 2013 to 2024.

The US, UK, EU and other governments attribute APT28 to Russia's military intelligence service, the GRU, specifically its 85th Main Special Service Center (military unit 26165). MITRE says the group has been active since at least 2004, and government advisories describe espionage against governments, militaries, political parties, media and logistics firms.

The US, UK and other governments have attributed APT29 to Russia's Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR). In April 2021 the US and UK attributed the 2020 SolarWinds Orion compromise to the SVR, and MITRE says the group has operated since at least 2008.

MITRE ATT&CK describes APT32 (OceanLotus) as a suspected Vietnam-based threat group active since at least 2014 that targets governments, dissidents, journalists and companies, mainly in Southeast Asia. CERT-EU calls it Vietnam-linked, but no government indictment or sanction names it. The latest dated activity in these sources is January 2025.

MITRE ATT&CK describes APT33 as a suspected Iranian threat group active since at least 2013, with a particular interest in aviation and energy in the United States, Saudi Arabia and South Korea. CERT-EU's March 2024 brief calls it an Iranian-linked cyberespionage group; no government indictment or sanction naming it was found.

MITRE ATT&CK describes OilRig, also tracked as APT34, as a suspected Iranian group working on behalf of the Iranian government since at least 2014, and the UAE Cyber Security Council issued advisories on it in October and December 2024. MITRE and the UAE council list government, energy, financial, chemical and telecoms targets mainly in the Middle East, reached through phishing emails and stolen logins.

MITRE ATT&CK describes APT35, also called Charming Kitten or Magic Hound, as an Iranian-sponsored espionage group likely working for the IRGC, and the UK NCSC and Germany's BfV describe its spear-phishing of academics, journalists, NGOs and critics of Iran. Start with multi-factor authentication on email and checking unexpected contact through another channel.

MITRE ATT&CK describes Transparent Tribe, also called APT36, as a suspected Pakistan-based threat group that has been active since at least 2013. It mainly targets diplomatic, defense and research organizations in India and Afghanistan with weaponized documents, lookalike websites and remote access trojans such as Crimson.

MITRE ATT&CK describes APT37, also called ScarCruft, as a North Korean state-sponsored cyber espionage group that has been active since at least 2012. It targets South Korea first, using spearphishing emails with Hangul (HWP) attachments, compromised websites and cloud services for control. No government advisory opened names the group itself.

APT38 is a North Korean state-sponsored group focused on financial theft, attributed by MITRE ATT&CK to North Korea's Reconnaissance General Bureau. MITRE lists banks, cryptocurrency exchanges and SWIFT system endpoints among its targets. The US Department of Justice named APT38 in November 2025 forfeiture cases over four 2023 cryptocurrency heists.

The US Treasury, FBI and Department of Justice attributed APT39, also called Chafer, to Iran's Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS), working through the front company Rana Intelligence Computing Company, in September 2020. The US sanctioned the company and 45 people.

APT40 (tracked by MITRE as Leviathan) is attributed by the US and UK governments (2021) and by agencies in eight countries (2024) to China's Ministry of State Security. The US charged four people in 2021, three of them named as officers of its Hainan State Security Department.

MITRE describes APT41 as a Chinese state-sponsored espionage group, as researchers have assessed it, that also runs financially motivated operations. The US Department of Justice charged five Chinese nationals in 2019 and 2020 and said the hacking reached more than 100 victims.

MITRE ATT&CK describes APT42 as an Iranian-sponsored threat group that conducts cyber espionage and surveillance, active since at least 2015. Israel's National Digital Agency says it works in line with the IRGC Intelligence Organization. The UK NCSC warned in 2023 about its patient spear-phishing of academics, officials, journalists and NGOs.

Google Threat Intelligence Group attributes the zero-day exploitation of BeyondTrust Remote Support (CVE-2026-102764), which it dates to late August 2026, to ARMORY CASTLE, a suspected China-linked spying group it formerly tracked as UNC5221. No government has named the group.

MITRE ATT&CK describes BITTER as a suspected South Asian cyber espionage group, active since at least 2013, that has targeted government, energy and engineering organizations in Pakistan, China, Bangladesh and Saudi Arabia. It sends spearphishing emails with malicious attachments and exploits known flaws in Microsoft Office.

Attributed by the US and Japanese governments (joint advisory, 27 September 2023) to cyber actors linked to the People's Republic of China, BlackTech is described as targeting government, technology, media, electronics and telecommunication organizations in East Asia and the US. It steals information, and the advisory details how it hides in router firmware to keep access.

CyberAv3ngers (also called Shahid Kaveh Group in a 2026 advisory) is attributed by US, Israeli, Canadian and UK agencies to the Iranian IRGC, and is tied to defacing internet-exposed industrial controllers at US water facilities from November 2023. A 2026 US advisory on Iranian-affiliated attacks on US industrial controllers refers to this group as earlier activity but does not say the two are the same.

Attributed by the US and UK governments to Russia's FSB Center 16 (Military Unit 71330), this group is tied to supply chain, phishing and website attacks on energy and industrial control system companies, and to the abuse of weak routers. Its work is espionage and lasting access to networks.

The US, UK, EU and Estonian governments attribute this activity to GRU Unit 29155, a Russian military intelligence unit, and MITRE tracks it as Ember Bear. It is described as using public tools and flaws in internet-facing systems to spy, leak data and wipe data, with a focus on Ukraine and those who aid it.

Attributed by the US Department of Justice to a financially motivated criminal conspiracy of dozens of computer specialists, FIN7 is described in US court papers as stealing tens of millions of payment card records from US businesses, and the FBI has warned about its mailed USB devices used to deliver ransomware. It hacks company networks to steal card data and, in later years, to deploy ransomware.

Attributed by Ukraine's Security Service (SSU, 2021) to Russia's FSB, and described by MITRE ATT&CK as a suspected Russian group that has targeted Ukrainian organizations since at least 2013. It mostly gets in through emails with Office files or archives, and a Ukrainian court convicted two members in absentia on 8 October 2024.

Attributed by the US and UK governments (19 July 2021) to the Chinese state, and charged by the US Department of Justice (8 July 2025) as directed by officers of China's Ministry of State Security, HAFNIUM is the name of the actor behind the campaign that exploited Microsoft Exchange Server flaws in early 2021. MITRE describes it as a likely state-sponsored espionage group that targets US universities, law firms, defense contractors and research bodies.

Handala Hack is a persona that MITRE ATT&CK lists under VOID MANTICORE (G1055). The group is assessed to operate on behalf of Iran's Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS). The US Department of Justice (19 March 2026) says the Handala domains were MOIS-controlled. The FBI (20 March 2026) assesses Handala Hack is linked to the Homeland Justice persona, also operated by MOIS cyber actors.

Attributed by MITRE ATT&CK to a Russia-based criminal group, which it also lists as Evil Corp. The US Treasury, the US Department of Justice and UK authorities name people behind the Dridex banking malware and later ransomware, and have sanctioned or charged them. Its work is stealing money from banks and extorting companies with ransomware.

k0t is a threat actor that Group-IB and NyxLab, in a joint report of 21 October 2026, describe as likely one of the main operators of a large campaign. The campaign targets exposed FortiGate, FortiWeb and Palo Alto GlobalProtect devices. They say current evidence suggests the operators are likely acting as initial access brokers, a role they have not confirmed.

Attributed by the US and South Korean governments to North Korea's Reconnaissance General Bureau, Kimsuky sends convincing fake emails to think tanks, researchers, media and government staff to steal documents and email. South Korea and the US Treasury sanctioned it in 2023, and the FBI reported new QR code phishing from it in 2025.

The US Cyber Safety Review Board describes Lapsus$ as a loosely organized, extortion-focused criminal group based mainly in the United Kingdom and Brazil, and UK and Brazilian police have made arrests in cases linked to it. It tricked staff, used stolen logins, and stole or deleted company data.

Attributed by the Dutch AIVD and MIVD (2025) and by US, UK, Canadian and other allied agencies (July 2026) to Russian state-supported actors, LAUNDRY BEAR steals email from government, defense and technology bodies. The July 2026 joint advisory describes a view-based attack on Zimbra webmail that took 90 days of mail without a click.

Lazarus Group is the name used by MITRE, the US Treasury and the US Department of Justice for North Korean hacking units. They say these units work for the Reconnaissance General Bureau. The US charged three RGB members in 2020 and 2021 with attempts to steal or extort more than $1.3 billion. The FBI attributed the 2025 Bybit theft to North Korean actors it tracks as TraderTraitor.

Attributed by the US, UK and EU governments to a China-based group working with the Ministry of State Security, menuPass (APT10) is known for reaching companies through their managed service providers. The US charged two people in December 2018 and the EU listed two people and a company in July 2020.

Japan's National Police Agency (NPA) and NISC (8 January 2025) describe MirrorFace (also called Earth Kasha) as an organized group with suspected Chinese involvement. It is reported to target Japanese think tanks, government, politicians, media, academia, and semiconductor, manufacturing and aerospace firms. It uses phishing emails and flaws in internet-facing devices to steal information on national security and advanced technology.

MITRE ATT&CK, the FBI, CISA, NCSC-UK and the US Treasury attribute this group to Iran's Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS). It is described as running cyber espionage against telecommunications, defense, local government and oil and gas organizations. The 2022 joint advisory says it gets in by spearphishing and known software flaws. It says the group shares access with other actors.

MITRE ATT&CK describes Mustang Panda as a China-based cyber espionage threat actor, and the US Department of Justice, citing court documents, says the PRC government paid the group to develop a version of PlugX. It is said to target governments, diplomats, think tanks and civil society through phishing emails with decoy documents.

MITRE ATT&CK attributes Salt Typhoon to the PRC state and says it has been active since at least 2019. Salt Typhoon compromised network equipment at major US telecommunications and internet providers. A joint advisory by 13 countries (27 August 2025) says PRC state-sponsored actors with partly overlapping activity mostly exploit known flaws in routers and edge devices. Patch and lock down those devices first.

The US, UK and EU governments attribute this group to Russian military intelligence (GRU Unit 74455). It is linked to the 2015 and 2016 power grid attacks in Ukraine, the 2017 NotPetya attack and the 2018 Winter Olympics attack. Its work is destructive: wipers and attacks on industrial control systems.

Scattered Spider is described by MITRE ATT&CK and by the FBI, CISA and partner agencies as a cybercriminal group that targets large companies and their IT help desks, mainly by tricking staff into resetting passwords and MFA. The UK National Crime Agency said on 16 July 2026 that its action against two leading members effectively halted the group, while others may reuse the name.

The FBI describes ShinyHunters as a cyber criminal group that specializes in large-scale data breaches and extortion, and Europol describes a coalition of it with Scattered Spider and LAPSUS$ called Scattered LAPSUS$ Hunters (SLSH). The US Department of Justice prosecuted a member in 2023 and 2024, and the Dutch National Police arrested a suspect in September 2026.

MITRE ATT&CK describes SideWinder as a suspected Indian threat actor group active since at least 2012. The national CERTs of Pakistan and Bangladesh, CERT-EU and ENISA report that it sends spearphishing emails to government, military and diplomatic bodies, mainly in South Asia. Sources differ on how sure they are about the India link, and none names a sponsor.

Silent Lynx is a cyber espionage group that targets government bodies in Central Asia and nearby countries. Cisco Talos, which tracks it as UAT-6275, assesses with medium confidence that it has a Kazakhstan nexus.

The UK, US, Australian, Canadian and New Zealand governments attribute this group to Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB) Center 18. It is linked to long phishing campaigns against politicians, researchers, journalists and government staff in the UK, US and other NATO countries. It steals email logins and reads the victims' mail.

CISA and the FBI say, "according to open source information", that the CL0P ransomware gang is also known as TA505, and MITRE ATT&CK describes TA505 as a cyber criminal group active since at least 2014. As attributed by those bodies, it steals data and runs ransomware, including through zero-day flaws in file transfer software such as MOVEit Transfer.

The US FBI (July 2026) describes TeamPCP as a cyber criminal group behind large-scale software supply chain compromises of widely used developer and security tools. Australian and US authorities announced arrests and an indictment linked to the group in August 2026, and MITRE ATT&CK describes it as active since at least September 2025.

Attributed by MITRE ATT&CK to Russia's FSB, Turla has run espionage against governments, embassies and the military since at least 2004. In May 2023 the US and partners attributed the Snake malware to a unit in FSB Center 16, and on 14 July 2026 the EU named the FSB 16th Center as controlling groups including Turla.

Singapore's cyber agency (CSA) calls UNC3886 a state-sponsored group without naming a state, and MITRE ATT&CK describes it as China-nexus, in entries dated 2025 and 2026. The group is reported to break into firewalls, routers and virtualization hosts for espionage, and CSA says it targeted all four major Singapore telecom operators.

Attributed by the US government and its Five Eyes partners to a People's Republic of China state-sponsored actor, Volt Typhoon is described in US advisories as pre-positioning inside critical infrastructure IT networks to be able to disrupt operations in a crisis. MITRE says it has been active since at least 2021.

Wizard Spider is a Russia-based criminal group behind the Trickbot malware, attributed by the US Department of Justice and Treasury, the UK government and Germany's BKA. Its work is stealing money and data and installing ransomware such as Ryuk and Conti. In 2023 the US charged nine members and the US and UK sanctioned 18 people.

8Base is the name of a ransomware affiliate group that used the Phobos ransomware. In February 2025 the US Justice Department said it had charged two Russian nationals who allegedly ran it, and that it had hit more than 1,000 public and private entities and received over 16 million US dollars in ransom payments. The department also said Europol and German authorities announced an operation against the network's servers.

Model: Ransomware affiliate group using Phobos (Phobos itself is a ransomware as a service)

Extortion: Double extortion, per the US Justice Department: the group allegedly stole files, encrypted the originals with Phobos, left a ransom note and contacted victims to negotiate. It threatened to expose stolen files to the public or to victims' clients, customers or constituents, and ran a darknet website where it published stolen data if a victim did not pay.

Akira is a ransomware group active since March 2023. A joint advisory (AA24-109A, first published April 18, 2024, revised 13 November 2025) from the FBI, CISA, Europol and agencies in France, Germany and the Netherlands says it has hit businesses and critical infrastructure in North America, Europe and Australia. As of late September 2025 it had claimed about 244.17 million US dollars in proceeds, per the advisory.

Model: Ransomware as a service (per MITRE ATT&CK)

Extortion: Double extortion, per the advisory: data is stolen first, then systems are encrypted and victims are threatened with a leak. The ransom note gives a unique code and a Tor address. No demand is left on the network. Payment is requested in Bitcoin.

ALPHV Blackcat is a ransomware as a service operation. The FBI, CISA and the US Department of Health and Human Services describe it in a joint advisory (AA23-353A, first issued December 19, 2023, revised 27 February 2024). Operators run the ransomware and affiliates carry out the attacks.

Model: Ransomware as a service

Extortion: Per the FBI, CISA and HHS: affiliates steal data, may or may not encrypt, and then contact victims through Tor, Tox, email or encrypted apps. Some affiliates extort victims without deploying ransomware at all. Victim-specific emails have been used to announce a compromise.

BianLian is a ransomware and data extortion group that the FBI, CISA and Australia's ACSC say is likely based in Russia. It has hit US and Australian organizations since June 2022 and, by about January 2024, had dropped encryption for pure data theft.

Model: Developer and deployer group with Russia-based affiliates

Extortion: Steals data, then threatens to publish it unless paid. It used to encrypt files too, but the agencies say it moved to data theft only around January 2024. Contact is through a Tox chat.

Black Basta is a ransomware as a service operation, first identified in April 2022. The FBI, CISA, HHS and MS-ISAC reported in a joint advisory (AA24-131A, first published May 10, 2024) that its affiliates had hit over 500 organizations worldwide by May 2024. Ransomware as a service means the core team rents its malware to partner criminals, called affiliates, who carry out the attacks.

Model: Ransomware as a service

Extortion: Double extortion, as the joint advisory describes it: affiliates encrypt systems and also steal data. The ransom note gives no price or payment steps. It gives the victim a unique code and a Tor address (a hidden site reached with the Tor browser), and typically allows 10 to 12 days to pay before the stolen data is published on the group's leak site, Basta News.

Cl0p is a ransomware operation first seen in February 2019 and, per a joint FBI and CISA advisory (AA23-158A, June 2023), also known as TA505. It is best known for stealing data from many organizations at once by exploiting flaws in file transfer software, including Accellion, GoAnywhere and MOVEit.

Model: Ransomware as a service, and data theft campaigns (per the advisory)

Extortion: Data theft first. Per the advisory, since 2021 Cl0p has relied mostly on exfiltration over encryption. Ransom notes go to senior executives of victim companies and threaten to publish the stolen files on the Cl0p leak site if no payment is made. Earlier campaigns also used double extortion.

Conti was a ransomware as a service operation first observed in December 2019, per MITRE ATT&CK. A joint advisory (AA21-265A) from CISA, the FBI and the NSA, first published September 22, 2021, says it hit U.S. and international organizations in more than 400 attacks at first and above 1,000 by March 2022. The U.S. Department of Justice says the conspiracy ran until about June 2022.

Model: Ransomware as a service, with a wage model per CISA

Extortion: Double extortion, per CISA: files are stolen and servers and workstations are encrypted. The victim is told to pay for the release of the data and is threatened with public release if it does not. Rewards for Justice says the stolen data is sold or published on a leak site if the ransom is not paid, and that some demands reached 25 million US dollars.

DarkSide was a ransomware as a service group that CISA and the FBI named in advisory AA21-131A, first published May 11, 2021, after an attack on a U.S. pipeline company's IT network. A later advisory (AA21-291A, October 18, 2021) says it was active from September 2020 through May 2021 and that BlackMatter is a possible rebrand.

Model: Ransomware as a service

Extortion: Double extortion, per CISA and the FBI: data is encrypted and stolen, then the actors threaten to release it if the ransom is not paid. The group publicly said it preferred organizations able to pay large ransoms over hospitals, schools, non-profits and governments.

DearCry is ransomware that CISA said, in a March 12, 2021 update, was being used on compromised on-premises Exchange servers. The servers had been broken into through the Exchange flaws disclosed in March 2021. The sources opened do not name who operated it.

Model: Ransomware family deployed after Exchange server compromise

DragonForce is a ransomware family that, per a July 29, 2025 update to a joint advisory from agencies including CISA, the FBI and the UK's NCSC, Scattered Spider actors have most recently been deploying. The update is attributed to trusted third parties. The UK's NCSC also names the DragonForce group in its 2025 annual review, in connection with attacks on UK retail.

Model: Not described in official sources

Extortion: The July 2025 advisory update says Scattered Spider actors typically steal data for extortion and also use several ransomware variants. It lists DragonForce as ransomware that infiltrates networks, encrypts data and demands a ransom. It adds that the actors may have deployed it to encrypt VMware ESXi servers.

Everest is a financially motivated ransomware and data extortion group. The US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) says it has been active since 2020, steals and threatens to publish data, runs ransomware, and also acts as an initial access broker, meaning it sells entry into company networks to other criminals.

Model: Extortion group with ransomware and initial access broker activity

Extortion: Data theft and ransomware, per HHS HC3 (August 2024): the group encrypts files, renames them with the .EVEREST extension and threatens to publish stolen data on its leak site. It has also sold network access to other actors.

Hive was a ransomware as a service operation active from June 2021. A joint advisory (AA22-321A) from the FBI, CISA and HHS says it hit over 1,300 companies and received about 100 million US dollars in ransom. The UK National Crime Agency reports its servers were taken offline in an FBI and German-led operation on 26 January 2023.

Model: Ransomware as a service

Extortion: Double extortion, per the advisory: data is copied out, then systems are encrypted. A note named HOW_TO_DECRYPT.txt links to a live chat panel on Tor. Victims who refuse are threatened with publication on the HiveLeaks site. Demands are in US dollars, paid in Bitcoin. Some victims were also contacted by phone or email.

Interlock is a ransomware group first observed in late September 2024. A joint advisory (AA25-203A, released July 22, 2025) from the FBI, CISA, HHS and MS-ISAC says it has hit businesses and critical infrastructure in North America and Europe, and that it often gets in through fake browser updates on compromised websites.

Model: Not stated in the advisory (opportunistic and financially motivated, per the FBI)

Extortion: Double extortion, per the advisory: data is stolen first, then systems are encrypted. The ransom note carries no demand, only a unique code and a Tor address. Payment is requested in Bitcoin. The actors threaten to publish stolen data on a leak site and have done so before.

KillSec is a ransomware and data extortion group that Europol says has been active since around 2024. On 30 September 2026 law enforcement took control of its leak site, securing at least 110 terabytes of data, in an operation led by German authorities.

Model: Data theft and extortion by a group whose suspected members held administrator, developer, negotiator and affiliate roles (attributed by Europol)

Extortion: Data theft and threats, per Europol: victims were named on the group's dark web leak site and threatened with publication of their data unless they paid. Where a victim did not pay, the stolen files could be made available for free download. In some cases the group obtained substantial ransom payments.

LockBit is a ransomware as a service operation first seen in January 2020. A joint advisory (AA23-165A, June 14, 2023) calls it the most deployed ransomware variant in the world in 2022. The UK National Crime Agency took control of its services in February 2024 and, in May 2024, assessed the group as running at limited capacity.

Model: Ransomware as a service

Extortion: Double extortion, per the advisory: affiliates encrypt data and also copy it out, then threaten to post it on leak sites. The advisory says leak sites show only part of the real victim count. The NCA says LockBit did not routinely delete stolen data after a ransom was paid.

Lynx is a ransomware group that the Cyber Security Agency of Singapore named on 16 August 2025 as one of at least eight groups using a tool that switches off endpoint security software. MITRE ATT&CK has no entry for it.

Model: Not stated in official sources

Extortion: The official sources cited on this page do not describe how Lynx extorts its victims.

Medusa is a ransomware-as-a-service operation first identified in June 2021, according to the FBI, CISA and HHS. As of April 2026 they count over 500 victims, with healthcare a frequent target. It steals data and encrypts files, then threatens to publish the data.

Model: Ransomware as a service (closed group until at least early 2023)

Extortion: Double extortion. Files are encrypted and stolen data is held for ransom. A leak site shows countdown timers, and a note gives 48 hours to make contact. The group may also phone or email victims.

Nefilim was a ransomware-as-a-service operation that stole data, encrypted networks and threatened to publish what it took. The US Department of Justice says its administrators gave affiliates access in return for a percentage of ransom payments; affiliate Artem Stryzhak agreed to pay 20%. On 27 October 2026 a US court sentenced him to 70 months in prison.

Model: Ransomware as a service with double extortion; affiliate Stryzhak agreed to pay the administrators 20% of ransom proceeds (per the US Department of Justice)

Extortion: Double extortion. The DOJ says Nefilim ransom notes typically threatened that, unless the victim came to an agreement, the stolen data would be published on public "Corporate Leaks" websites kept by the Nefilim administrators. The DOJ says victims who paid received a decryption key. In its plea release it adds that a unique ransomware file, with its own key and ransom note, was made for each victim.

Play, also called Playcrypt, is a ransomware group active since June 2022. A joint advisory (AA23-352A, December 18, 2023, revised 4 June 2025) from the FBI, CISA and the Australian Cyber Security Centre says it was among the most active groups in 2024 and that, as of May 2025, the FBI knew of about 900 affected entities.

Model: Closed group (presumed, per the advisory)

Extortion: Double extortion: data is stolen, then systems are encrypted. Notes carry no demand, only an email address. Victims who refuse are threatened with publication on a Tor leak site, and some are phoned.

Qilin, also tracked as Agenda, is a ransomware as a service family that MITRE ATT&CK says has been active since at least 2022. It has Go and Rust versions that target Windows, Linux and VMware ESXi. Ransomware as a service means the core team rents its malware to partner criminals, called affiliates.

Model: Ransomware as a service

Extortion: Double extortion, per MITRE ATT&CK: the operators demand payment for decryption keys and for not publishing stolen data on their leak site. They also run a Telegram news channel to announce Qilin activity.

RansomHub is a ransomware as a service operation, formerly known as Cyclops and Knight, according to a joint advisory (AA24-242A) from the FBI, CISA, MS-ISAC and HHS released on August 29, 2024. The advisory says it had encrypted and stolen data from at least 210 victims since its start in February 2024. Ransomware as a service means the core team rents its malware to partner criminals, called affiliates.

Model: Ransomware as a service

Extortion: Double extortion, per the advisory: affiliates encrypt systems and steal data. The ransom note gives a client ID and a unique Tor address (a hidden site reached with the Tor browser) rather than a price. It typically allows between three and 90 days, depending on the affiliate, before data is published on the RansomHub leak site.

REvil, also called Sodinokibi, is a ransomware as a service operation that MITRE ATT&CK says ran since at least April 2019. The U.S. Department of Justice says it was used in thousands of attacks, including the July 2021 attack on Kaseya, an IT software company, that reached its customers. Between November 2021 and May 2024 the United States sanctioned, charged, extradited and sentenced people tied to it.

Model: Ransomware as a service

Extortion: Double extortion, per the Department of Justice: data was encrypted and victims who did not pay saw their data exposed. Ransoms were demanded in cryptocurrency, and the group used exchangers and mixing services to hide the proceeds. Treasury says the group received more than 200 million US dollars in Bitcoin and Monero.

Rhysida is a ransomware operation that CISA, the FBI and the MS-ISAC say has mainly been deployed against education, healthcare, manufacturing, IT and government organizations since May 2023. Open source reporting describes it as a ransomware-as-a-service model where any ransom is split with associates. Rhysida uses double extortion: victims pay to decrypt files and pay again to stop stolen data being published.

Model: Ransomware as a service (profit-sharing with associates)

Extortion: Double extortion. Victims are told to pay in Bitcoin both to decrypt files and to stop stolen data being published. A PDF ransom note points to a Tor portal.

Royal is a ransomware group that, according to a joint FBI and CISA advisory (AA23-061A, first published March 2, 2023), rebranded as BlackSuit. The advisory says BlackSuit is the evolution of Royal and shares numerous coding similarities with it. In August 2025 the US Justice Department announced the takedown of BlackSuit (Royal) servers and domains.

Model: Not stated as ransomware as a service in the sources; operated by the group itself

Extortion: Double extortion, per the advisory: data is stolen before encryption, then published to a leak site if the ransom is not paid. The ransom note holds no amount. Victims must contact the actors through a Tor address. The advisory also reports phone and email contact with victims.

SafePay is a ransomware group that the FBI, CISA and partners say has been highly active since August 2024. A joint advisory published on 20 October 2026 counts at least 600 separate victims, from multiple critical infrastructure sectors.

Model: Data theft and encryption, then a threat to publish the data on a leak site (per advisory AA26-293A)

Extortion: Double extortion in effect: data is copied out before encryption, and data of victims who do not pay is posted on the SafePay leak site. The ransom note says SafePay locked the system and points to a chat portal on a TOR address, where the victim logs in with an ID. The advisory says a representative also makes phone calls to pressure the victim, and that actors typically demand a subset of company revenue in cryptocurrency.

The Gentlemen is a ransomware-as-a-service operation. Sophos says the scheme started in mid-2025 and posted its first victims to a leak site in September 2025. Unit 42 cites an outside count of 580 claimed victims in 77 countries through 7 July 2026. Check Point says entry is almost always through an unpatched internet-facing device such as a VPN or firewall.

Model: Ransomware as a service with double extortion; affiliates keep 90% of each ransom (per Unit 42, Sophos and Check Point)

Extortion: Double extortion in effect. Sophos and Trend Micro say the group steals data and encrypts files, then threatens to publish the data of victims who do not pay on its leak site. Check Point's DFIR report says the ransom note opens with "Gentlemen, your network has been encrypted." It tells victims who get no reply within 36 hours to create another account and write again. Negotiation runs through Tox or Session.

Vice Society is an intrusion, exfiltration and extortion group that first appeared in summer 2021, per joint advisory AA22-249A (FBI, CISA and MS-ISAC, September 6, 2022). The advisory says its actors disproportionately targeted the education sector and used other groups' ransomware rather than their own.

Model: Not stated in the advisory

Extortion: Double extortion, per the advisory: data is copied out before ransomware is deployed, and victims are threatened with public release of sensitive data unless they pay. The advisory lists a Tor address and OnionMail email accounts as indicators.

Warlock is a ransomware family that Microsoft says a China-based actor it tracks as Storm-2603 deployed in July 2025 after exploiting on-premises SharePoint servers. CISA's alert on the same flaws says actors were seen encrypting files and distributing Warlock on compromised systems.

Model: Not stated by the sources

Extortion: The opened sources describe file encryption and distribution of the ransomware through Group Policy. They do not describe a leak site or ransom note, so none is claimed here.

AcidRain is a wiper built as an ELF program for modems and routers that use MIPS processors. MITRE ATT&CK says it is associated with the KA-SAT satellite communication outage at the start of the 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine. It wipes the file system and storage devices and then reboots the device.

Akira is ransomware that locks files on a victim network and is used to demand payment. CISA and its partners describe an operation that also steals data first and threatens to publish it. Versions exist for Windows and for VMware ESXi virtual machines.

Amadey is a Windows loader that downloads and runs other malware on infected PCs, and criminals buy it as a service. MITRE says it has been used since at least October 2018. In June 2026 Eurojust, Microsoft and ESET announced an action against its control servers as part of Operation Endgame.

Bad Rabbit is self-propagating ransomware for Windows. MITRE ATT&CK says it affected the Ukrainian transportation sector in 2017 and also targeted organizations and consumers in Russia. The UK government attributes the October 2017 attack to the GRU, Russia's military intelligence service.

BARECLAW is a tunneler written in C that Google Threat Intelligence Group says a suspected China-nexus espionage group ran on a BeyondTrust Remote Support appliance in 2026. It turns the appliance into a hidden SOCKS5 proxy into the victim network.

Black Basta is ransomware, offered to criminal affiliates as a service, that encrypts files on Windows and VMware ESXi systems and steals data to pressure victims into paying. CISA and its partners say it was first identified in April 2022 and had affected over 500 organizations by May 2024.

BlackCat is ransomware written in Rust that was offered to criminal affiliates as a ransomware-as-a-service. MITRE says it was first observed in November 2021, and it can encrypt Windows devices, Linux devices and VMware instances. In December 2023 the US Justice Department announced a disruption campaign against the group behind it.

BlackEnergy is a malware toolkit for Windows. MITRE ATT&CK says it dates back to at least 2007 and was first built to create botnets for DDoS attacks, and that its use grew to support plug-ins. It was found on the networks of Ukrainian power companies in December 2015, though CISA says it could not confirm that BlackEnergy caused the outages.

BRICKSTORM is a backdoor that hides on VMware vCenter servers, ESXi hosts and network appliances. CISA, the NSA and the Canadian Cyber Centre assess that PRC state-sponsored cyber actors use it for long-term persistence on victim systems, mainly in the government services and information technology sectors. Google Threat Intelligence Group attributes the activity to UNC5221 and closely related, suspected China-nexus clusters.

CaddyWiper is destructive malware for Windows that overwrites files and drive structures. CISA says its purpose is to destroy user data so the victim cannot reach it. MITRE says it has been used in attacks on organizations in Ukraine since at least March 2022.

Candiru spyware is surveillance software made by Candiru, an Israeli company that the Citizen Lab says sells spyware only to governments. In October 2026 the Citizen Lab said, with high confidence, that this spyware infected devices at an international news network through targeted online ads that needed no click.

CanisterWorm is a self-propagating worm that steals cloud and developer credentials and uses stolen npm tokens to push itself into more software packages. MITRE says it has a wiper part aimed at Kubernetes and Iranian systems, and that it can fetch payload locations from a blockchain canister. The FBI lists it among the malware deployed by the cyber criminal group TeamPCP.

China Chopper is a small web shell that attackers place on a web server to get remote access to it. It has a client the attacker runs and a server part that sits on the victim server. UK and partner agencies describe it as a publicly available tool used by hostile actors to manage files and open a terminal on compromised web servers.

Clop is ransomware for Windows that locks files and adds its own file extension. MITRE says it was first observed in February 2019 and is a variant of the CryptoMix ransomware. CISA and the FBI describe the CL0P gang as using it for extortion, and in later campaigns mostly stealing data instead of encrypting it.

Cobalt Strike is a commercial remote access tool sold for adversary simulation, which means security teams use it to test their own networks. CISA, the FBI and the NCSC also report attackers using it after a break-in to control machines, move across the network and take data. Its main payload is called Beacon.

Conti is ransomware that steals a victim's files, encrypts Windows systems and then demands payment. MITRE describes it as a ransomware as a service operation first observed in December 2019. US agencies counted more than 1,000 attacks by February 2022.

Crimson RAT is a remote access trojan for Windows. MITRE ATT&CK lists the group Transparent Tribe (APT36) as the user and says the group has used it since at least 2016. It can log keystrokes, capture screens, webcam video and audio, and collect files, including from removable drives.

CROSSROAD is the name Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant give to a downloader used in a 2026 tampering of AOMEI Backupper updates. It ran on a computer when the backup program fetched a tampered update, then set up a backdoor that they name SHINYROAD.

Cyclops Blink is modular malware that runs on small office and home office network devices, mainly WatchGuard devices. The UK and US governments say it has been deployed since at least June 2019 and attribute it to the Sandworm actor. It appears to replace the VPNFilter malware, and a US court-authorized operation cut part of its command layer off in March 2022.

Derusbi is malware that MITRE ATT&CK says is used by multiple Chinese APT groups. Both Windows and Linux variants have been observed. MITRE records abilities such as logging keystrokes, capturing screen, audio and video, running a remote shell and deleting files.

Dtrack is spyware for Windows that MITRE ATT&CK says was discovered in 2019. MITRE says it has been used against Indian financial institutions, research facilities and the Kudankulam Nuclear Power Plant. MITRE lists Lazarus Group as a user and notes similarities with the DarkSeoul campaign.

Emotet is a modular Windows malware that began as a banking Trojan and became a loader, a tool that installs other malware such as banking Trojans or ransomware. It mostly arrives in phishing emails with malicious attachments or links. Law enforcement took control of its infrastructure in January 2021.

Evilginx is a free, open source toolkit that sits between a victim and a real website and copies what passes through, including passwords and login session cookies. It was built for security testing, but attackers also use it to take over accounts and get around multifactor authentication that is not phishing resistant. MITRE tracks it as evilginx2.

FASTCash is the name the US Government gives to an ATM cash-out scheme and the malware behind it. The malware runs on a bank payment switch server, reads card request messages and sends back fake approvals, so cash can leave ATMs in many countries at once.

gh0st RAT is a remote access tool for Windows and macOS. MITRE ATT&CK says its source code is public and that multiple groups have used it. It can open a remote shell, log keystrokes, capture the screen and download more files.

GlassWorm is a worm that targets developer tools. MITRE says it compromises repository credentials and adds malicious payloads to those accounts. It was first reported in October 2025 in VS Code extensions. In October 2026 StepSecurity tied its loader to a swapped release of the OVHcloud command line tool.

HOOKEDGE is a lightweight Windows backdoor made of batch scripts, delivered through Word documents that carry a macro. It takes its commands from the webhook.site service and sends the results back to it. Recorded Future's Insikt Group attributes it with moderate confidence to BlueDelta, which overlaps with APT28. Symantec's researchers found it in attacks on organizations in two NATO countries.

HOPLIGHT is a backdoor Trojan for Windows. MITRE ATT&CK says it has reportedly been used by the North Korean government. CISA and the FBI published an analysis report on it in April 2019, and a 2020 joint advisory said the US Government had found it on victim systems, which suggested a bank-targeting group was using it.

Impacket is a free, open source set of Python modules for working with network protocols. It includes tools for running commands on remote machines, dumping Windows credentials, working with Kerberos tickets, sniffing traffic and relaying logins. Defenders see it mostly because attackers, including state actors and ransomware groups named in CISA advisories, use it once they are inside a network.

Industroyer, also called CrashOverride, is a malware framework built to disrupt industrial control systems, specifically parts used in electrical substations. MITRE ATT&CK says it was used in the attacks on the Ukrainian power grid in December 2016. It is described as the first publicly known malware specifically designed to affect operations in the electric grid.

Infamous Chisel is a collection of components that targets Android devices. A joint report of 31 August 2023 says it was used by the actor Sandworm in a campaign against Android devices used by the Ukrainian military. It gives lasting remote access over the Tor network and regularly collects and sends out information from the device.

Kazuar is a backdoor Trojan that runs on Windows and macOS. MITRE ATT&CK describes it as fully featured and written in .NET. MITRE lists the Turla group as a user, and CERT-EU reported in 2024 and 2025 that Turla used versions of it against targets in Ukraine.

KV Botnet is malware that took over small office and home office routers and linked them into a botnet. The US Department of Justice says Chinese state-sponsored hackers used it to hide where their attacks on critical infrastructure came from. A court-authorized operation disrupted it in December 2023, and the US announced this on 31 January 2024.

LAPLAS is a Windows implant used by the group Silent Lynx. Cisco Talos calls it a lightweight reverse shell. Seqrite describes a C++ implant with TCP and TLS versions that talks to the operators' servers.

Mimikatz is a tool that pulls Windows account logins and passwords out of a computer. MITRE describes it as a credential dumper that is also useful for testing the security of networks. The UK NCSC says it was not originally meant as a hacking tool, but hostile actors now use it widely once they have access to a host.

Mini Shai-Hulud is a credential stealer and self-replicating worm that spreads through software packages and build pipelines. MITRE says it derives from Shai-Hulud and that the group TeamPCP has used it against CI/CD workflows. It steals cloud, container and developer credentials and uses stolen publishing tokens to push itself into more packages.

NICECURL is a backdoor written in VBScript. MITRE ATT&CK lists APT42 as the user and says it downloads additional modules. MITRE says it gives the operator an interface to run commands, talks to its server over HTTPS and can remove its own artifacts.

NotPetya is destructive malware that looks like ransomware. MITRE says the attackers never intended the encrypted data to be recoverable, so it is better thought of as a wiper. It spread across networks from 27 June 2017 and has been attributed by the UK, the US and others to the Russian military.

Olympic Destroyer is a Windows wiper that was used against computers supporting the 2018 Winter Olympics in Pyeongchang, South Korea. MITRE ATT&CK says its main purpose was to render infected systems inoperable, and that it has worm-like features to spread across a network. The US Department of Justice and the UK government attribute the attack to the Russian GRU unit known as Sandworm.

PEERSTITCH is a small Linux program that Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 found on Fortinet FortiGate firewalls. It injects code into two running system processes and leaves no file on disk. Unit 42 ties it to an intrusion that began with a FortiManager flaw.

PickleShell is a lightweight reverse shell on Windows. It lets an operator type commands on an infected PC from afar. Cisco Talos found it in campaigns against government bodies in Central Asia and nearby countries, which it attributes to the cluster UAT-6275. Talos says this cluster overlaps with Silent Lynx (first reported by Seqrite).

PlugX is a remote access tool for Windows, built from plugins. It lets an operator run commands, capture screens and keystrokes, and move files on an infected computer. MITRE lists many threat groups that have used it, and the FBI has observed it since at least 2012.

PoisonIvy is a remote access tool (RAT) for Windows that MITRE describes as popular and used by many groups. It gives an attacker a backdoor to a computer, with a command line, file upload, keylogging and window title capture. A US indictment of two APT10 members names it among the malware installed through spear phishing emails.

RedLine Stealer is information-stealing malware that MITRE says was first identified in 2020. It takes saved browser passwords, cookies, card details and cryptocurrency wallet data from infected Windows computers. It was sold to criminals as a service, and in October 2024 an international police operation took down its servers.

REvil, also called Sodinokibi and Sodin, is ransomware for Windows. It encrypts files and demands a ransom to get them back. MITRE describes it as a ransomware-as-a-service operation that has run since at least April 2019, and says it has been used against organizations in the manufacturing, transportation and electric sectors.

ROKRAT is a cloud-based remote access tool for Windows. MITRE ATT&CK lists APT37, which it describes as a North Korean state-sponsored espionage group, as the user and says it was used against victims in South Korea in several campaigns from 2016 through 2021. It can log keystrokes, take screenshots, record audio and steal browser credentials, and it uses cloud and social networking services to reach its operators.

ROMULUS is a ClickFix delivery platform that Forescout's Vedere Labs described on 15 October 2026. One backend serves several payloads, including LegionLoader and a DLL side-loading chain that Huntress had reported. Siemens names a Romulus ClickFix campaign in its warning about CVE-2026-110936.

SAWFLY is a small PHP web shell that Google Threat Intelligence Group says a suspected China-nexus espionage group used on BeyondTrust Remote Support appliances in 2026. It hides its commands in encrypted traffic and stays silent when a request lacks the right parameter.

ShadowPad is a modular backdoor for Windows. MITRE ATT&CK says it was first identified in a supply chain compromise of NetSarang software in mid-July 2017. MITRE also says it has since been seen in use by various Chinese threat activity groups.

Shai-Hulud is a self-replicating worm that spreads through npm packages and code repositories. It steals credentials and access tokens from developer and build accounts, then uses them to publish infected package versions. CISA reported over 500 npm packages compromised in September 2025.

SHINYROAD is the name Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant give to a backdoor installed after a tampered AOMEI Backupper update in 2026. It hides inside the files of a genuine remote administration tool and can run code that its operators send.

Snake, also called Uroburos, is a cyber espionage implant written in C, with versions for Windows, Linux and macOS. US and allied agencies attribute it to a unit in Center 16 of Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB), which they say used it for long-term intelligence collection. It hides on the host, and its infected machines form a covert peer-to-peer network that relays stolen data.

SUNBURST is a trojanized Windows DLL built to fit inside the SolarWinds Orion software update framework. CISA describes it as a backdoor that lets a remote operator run functions on the system, deploy more payloads and exfiltrate data. In April 2021 the US and UK governments attributed the SolarWinds compromise to Russia's Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR).

TAMECAT is a PowerShell backdoor that MITRE ATT&CK lists as used by APT42 to run PowerShell or C# content. The Israel National Digital Agency describes it as a modular backdoor that runs mostly in memory and collects files, browser data, screenshots and Outlook mail, and says it can talk to its operators over HTTPS, Telegram and Discord.

TeamPCP Cloud Stealer is a credential stealer that checks more than 50 file paths on build servers, cloud accounts and developer machines. It encrypts what it finds and sends it out, with a fallback that uses the victim's own GitHub account. MITRE says TeamPCP used it as its main payload in March 2026, and the FBI uses the name SANDCLOCK for the same tool.

TruffleHog is a legitimate open source tool that searches for leaked passwords, API keys and other secrets in code, logs, chats and cloud storage. It is not malware. MITRE lists it as software because attackers can run it to find credentials, and CERT-EU reports that an actor launched it during the European Commission cloud breach in March 2026.

Ulej (Russian for beehive) is a custom data theft capability that the joint advisory AA26-204A describes as used by the Russian state-supported group LAUNDRY BEAR against Zimbra Collaboration Suite webmail. When a user views a malicious email in a vulnerable version, it attempts to send the last 90 days of email, the address directory and account secrets to servers running a collection framework called Flowerbed.

VersaMem is a web shell that MITRE ATT&CK says was built for Versa Director servers, which help manage SD-WAN networks. It is a Java Archive that captures logon credentials and can run further Java payloads. MITRE lists it as used by Volt Typhoon in a zero-day campaign against ISPs and MSPs in 2024.

WannaCry is ransomware that spreads on its own across a network like a worm and encrypts the files it finds. MITRE says it was first seen in a global attack in May 2017 that affected more than 150 countries. The US and UK governments have attributed that attack to North Korean actors.

OS credential dumping is when an attacker pulls account login material out of a computer. This is usually a password hash, sometimes a clear text password. The attacker can then use it to move to other systems and reach restricted information.

Data from local system is when an attacker searches a computer they already control to find files and other data worth taking. This usually happens before the data is sent out of the network. It can cover documents, settings files, databases and more.

Remote Services is when an attacker uses a valid account to log in to a service built for remote access, such as SSH, RDP or VNC. Once in, the attacker can act as that user. It is a common way to move from one system to another inside a network.

Obfuscated Files or Information is a technique where an attacker hides the real content of a file, program or command by encrypting, encoding or packing it. The goal is to slip past security tools and make analysis harder. Tools look for known patterns, so changing how content looks can stop the patterns matching while it still runs.

Masquerading is when an attacker changes how a file, program, service or account looks so it seems legitimate. They may change its name, where it sits or its descriptive details. The aim is to avoid being noticed by people and by security tools.

Exfiltration over a C2 channel is when an attacker sends stolen data out through the same channel they already use to control the infected system. The data is hidden inside what looks like normal control traffic, so no second route out of the network is needed. MITRE ATT&CK tracks it as T1041 under Exfiltration.

Scheduled Task/Job is a technique where an attacker uses the task scheduling feature built into an operating system. The feature runs a program or script at a set time or on a repeat. Attackers use it to start malicious code, to keep their access after a restart, or to run code with higher privileges.

Process injection is when an attacker runs their own code inside another program that is already running. The code then borrows the identity of that program. This can help it avoid security tools and, in some cases, gain more access.

Input capture is when an attacker records what a user types or enters, to steal passwords or other information. It can happen silently in the background or by tricking the user into typing into a fake prompt or page. MITRE lists four forms: keylogging, GUI input capture, web portal capture and credential API hooking.

Process Discovery is a technique where attackers list the programs running on a system. The result tells them what software is present and helps them decide what to do next, for example whether to fully infect the target. MITRE tracks it as T1057 under the Discovery tactic.

Command and Scripting Interpreter is a technique where an attacker uses the built-in shells and scripting languages of a system to run commands, scripts or programs. Most systems already include these tools, so the activity can look like normal administration.

Exploitation for privilege escalation is when an attacker uses a flaw in software to gain higher permissions than they started with. For example, they may go from a normal user account to full control of the system. The flaw can be in the operating system, in software running with higher permissions, or in a signed driver. MITRE ATT&CK tracks it as T1068.

Indicator Removal is a technique where an attacker deletes or changes the traces that their activity leaves behind. These traces include logs, command histories and file details. The aim is to blend in with normal activity and make the intrusion harder to spot.

Application Layer Protocol is a technique where attackers talk to a system they control using ordinary network protocols, such as those used for web browsing, file transfer, email or DNS. Because the traffic looks like normal traffic, it is harder to spot and block. MITRE tracks it as T1071 under the Command and Control tactic.

Valid Accounts means an attacker logs in with real credentials that were stolen or bought. Because the login is genuine, the activity can look like a normal user. MITRE says the access can be used to get in, stay in the network, gain higher privileges or avoid detection, so defenders watch how an account behaves.

System Information Discovery is when an attacker collects details about a device, such as its operating system version, patch level and hardware. The attacker uses this to decide what to do next on that device. It is a Discovery technique in MITRE ATT&CK.

File and Directory Discovery is a technique where an attacker lists files and folders on a system or a network share to learn what is there. The results help the attacker decide what to do next, such as which data to take.

Account Discovery is when an attacker builds a list of valid accounts, usernames or email addresses on a system or inside a compromised environment. Knowing which accounts exist helps them plan what to do next. MITRE ATT&CK lists it as a Discovery technique.

A dead drop resolver is a page on a legitimate web service that holds the address of the attacker's real command and control server. Malware reads the page, learns where to connect and can be pointed elsewhere by changing the page. MITRE tracks this as T1102.001.

Ingress Tool Transfer is a technique where attackers bring tools or other files from outside into a network they have already broken into. The files are used for later steps of the attack. They can arrive through the attacker's control channel, FTP or other protocols, often using utilities the operating system already includes. MITRE ATT&CK tracks it as T1105.

Modify Registry is a technique where an attacker changes settings in the Windows Registry. The Registry holds configuration for the system and its software. Changes can help an attacker stay on a machine, hide data or weaken security settings. MITRE ATT&CK tracks it as T1112 under Defense Impairment and Persistence.

External Remote Services is a technique where an attacker uses a remote access service that faces the internet, such as a VPN or Citrix, to enter a network or to keep access to it. These services exist so staff can reach internal systems from outside. An attacker who gets valid logins can use them in the same way.

Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information is a technique where attackers unpack, decode or decrypt content they had hidden earlier, so it can be used on the target system. The malware itself or built-in system utilities can do the work. MITRE tracks it as T1140 under the Stealth tactic.

Drive-by Compromise is a way for attackers to gain access to a computer when a person visits a website during normal browsing. The site, or something it loads, delivers malicious code to the browser. MITRE ATT&CK lists it as an Initial Access technique.

Exploit Public-Facing Application is when an attacker abuses a weakness in a system that is reachable from the Internet to get into a network. The weakness can be a software bug, a temporary glitch or a misconfiguration. It is an Initial Access technique.

Compromise Software Supply Chain is a way for attackers to reach many computers through software they already trust. They change an application before it gets to the user, for example in its source code, its update system or its download. MITRE ATT&CK lists it as an Initial Access technique.

User Execution is when an attacker gets a person to run malicious code for them. The person might open a file, click a link or turn on a remote access tool without knowing the risk. It is an Execution technique in MITRE ATT&CK.

Malicious Copy and Paste lets an attacker run code without an exploit and without a browser download. The user pastes the command into a terminal or the Windows Run box. MITRE names ClickFix, where a fake error or CAPTCHA tells the user to do exactly that, as one such strategy.

Data Encrypted for Impact is when attackers encrypt files or whole systems so the owner can no longer use them, and then hold back the key. It is the core step of ransomware. MITRE ATT&CK lists it as an Impact technique.

Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion is when malware checks whether it is running inside a virtual machine or an analysis sandbox, and changes what it does if it is. The aim is to avoid being studied. MITRE lists it under both Stealth and Discovery.

A web shell is a small script that an attacker places on a web server. It lets the attacker run commands on that server from a distance. Because it sits on the server itself, it keeps working even if the first way in is closed, which is why attackers use it to keep access to the network over time.

Python Startup Hooks let an attacker run code every time Python starts. A file dropped into the Python packages folder is processed by the interpreter itself, so the code runs even if the program never imports anything from it. MITRE tracks this as T1546.018.

Boot or logon autostart execution is when an attacker sets up a computer so that their program starts by itself when the system boots or a user logs on. This lets the attacker stay on the system after a restart. Some of these startup items run with higher privileges, so it can also help the attacker gain more control.

Windows can start programs on its own when a user logs in. Attackers add their own program to the places that control this, the Registry run keys or the Startup folder. The program then starts again after every restart or logon.

Credentials in Files means an attacker reads passwords, keys and tokens that sit in ordinary files on a disk or a file share. Config files, .env files and cloud credential files are common targets. The stolen secret is then used to sign in somewhere else. MITRE tracks it as T1552.001.

Credentials from password stores is when an attacker looks in the places where passwords are saved and takes the logins they find. These places include system password storage, saved browser logins, password managers and cloud secrets vaults. Stolen logins can then be used to move to other systems.

Archive collected data is when an attacker packs stolen files into compressed or encrypted bundles before sending them out. This makes the data smaller and harder for a defender to read or notice. The attacker can use a utility already on the system, a third party library or a custom method. MITRE ATT&CK tracks it as T1560 under Collection.

Hide Artifacts is a technique where attackers hide the traces of their activity, such as files, folders, user accounts or running tasks. The aim is to avoid being noticed by users and security tools. Attackers abuse operating system features that already hide items, so what is hidden is harder to find during a routine check. MITRE ATT&CK tracks it as T1564.

Phishing is when an attacker sends a message that tricks someone into opening a malicious file, following a link or giving away a password. It is a common first step into a network. Defenders check attachments and links before delivery, use multi-factor authentication and make it easy for staff to report suspicious messages.

Encrypted Channel is a technique where attackers encrypt the traffic they use to control a compromised system. The encryption hides what is being sent, so security tools that read network traffic see only scrambled data. MITRE ATT&CK tracks it as T1573 under Command and Control, and lists Emotet, gh0st RAT and NETWIRE as using it.

DLL hijacking is when an attacker abuses the shared library files (DLLs) that Windows programs load. A trusted program is made to load a harmful DLL instead of, or alongside, the real one. This helps the attacker stay in place, gain higher privileges and avoid detection.

Reflective code loading is a way for malware to run a program straight from memory, without starting a new process or putting the program on disk as a normal file. The payload can stay encrypted until the moment it runs. MITRE ATT&CK lists it as a Stealth technique.
